rv.q: Here is death: slight and bird-boned, gray-haired and sharp-eyed, wearing a blood-stained pink T-shirt and sensible shoes, still deeply, dreadfully in love with her old friend’s husband, still feeling inadequate in comparison to that friend, still full of longing and sorrow and life.
Luckily, these mesmerizing performers could keep us enthralled through any of the cataclysmic events alluded to in the play.

“A simmering, ultimately searing drama by Kirkwood...Superb three-member cast...A quiet but exquisitely well-observed slice of life, set in an all-too-easily foreseeable future, when life itself has become, well, more thinly sliced...MacDonald calibrates the play’s subdued but unmistakable nuggets of conflict expertly...
Having lived through an era of unprecedented peace and prosperity, Kirkwood’s characters are forced to confront the truth that all their efforts have bequeathed a blighted planet to their children.
Caryl Churchill's latest play is a masterpiece of economy and precision, building to a devastating climax that feels both inevitable and shocking.
Behind the subtleties of its direction and acting, The Children's central question is blunt: What does it mean to be responsible?
Ultimately, this is a difficult piece of theater, and the ambiguous though beautiful ending (with evocative lighting by Peter Mumford) presents so many implications it makes the head spin.

One of the astonishments of “The Children,” which comes to the Manhattan Theater Club intact from a run at the Theater in London last winter, is that even though it is completely successful as an eco-thriller, bristling with chills and suspense and foreboding sound effects, denuclearization is not its subject.
This is too facile, too familiar and too unexamined.
But the actors’ fine efforts are not enough to fully breathe life into this willfully slow-paced, sluggish work, which treats minor domestic issues and the future of the planet with equal gravity.
That swirling unknown is bought startlingly to life at the end of the play, in one of the most visually stunning denouements on Broadway right now.
Yes, 'The Children' is hardly child's play. But for thoughtful adults, it's required viewing.

That intact transfer is a fortuitous one, resulting in a polished ensemble piece that captures a sense of the characters' history, both as they relate to each other and as they are representative of the aging cohort of baby boomers to which they belong.
The Children is indeed to be savored for its fine writing, direction, and acting.
The visually stylized, well-acted production is directed by James Macdonald.

James Macdonald directs an extraordinary trio of actors.
The gabby beginnings of The Children rather magically inform a climax of life and death stakes.
The three actors, reprising roles from the Theatre run in London, deliver lived-in, persuasive performances.
Playwright Kirkwood seems to agree; it's the deceptive ordinariness of it all that makes "The Children" so deeply unnerving.
It helps too that much of the squabbling and banter is amusing.
For all its dramatic circumstances, The Children is not nearly as intense as its outline suggests.
Beautifully rendered, none of it adds up to the sustained tension that this play demands.
As the play concludes, however, the story collapses in on itself.
The Children, for all its mystery and topicality, doesn’t begin to rank with the others.

Regrettably, the most provocative thought The Children has left me with is the gnawing concern that plays of its kind will not do anymore, that the mounting crises of our world can no longer fit inside a box set, however oddly canted or dressed up with effects.

Kirkwood structures her compassionate, heart-wrenching treatise on social responsibility with such craft, you become wrapped up in the interrelations of this trio without even realizing they are symbols of modern society.
Perhaps this play fared better with more intellectual British audiences, but here on Broadway audiences often want something a bit more stimulating.
A play designed to disturb ends up producing an oddly lulling effect.
What is truly marvelous is the gap between the comfortable dialogue between the twosome, and then the threesome, and the emotions snaking around and under them.
Refreshingly real, these people are more function like the rest of us, obsessing more over dinner and yoga than fusion theory.

The atmosphere within that off-balanced living space in that old English cottage is downright tense. There is a bloody strong animosity hanging over these two older women as they politely play catch up in the Theatre transfer of the play, The Children by Lucy Kirkwood (2017. National’s The Mosquitoes).
The imagery of the play, both in the physical setting and the playwright’s words, is stark and memorable.
Even with its occasional sluggish moments and some difficulty understanding the coastal English dialect, The Children has a fearful universality that lingers in the mind.
Under James Macdonald’s purposive and gentle direction, “The Children” raises significant enduring questions left for the audience to grapple with.
Mostly, it is the expertise of the three cast members that keeps us glued.
“The Children” made a disturbing enough statement about the price we may pay in the future because of how we treat the present to merit further consideration.
For those of us watching from afar and hoping someday to be in the room, they stand as reminders of theatre at its most communal and most alive.
The Children is the most adult show in New York City right now, a marvelously resonant, intelligent, and engaging play.
At nearly two hours long without an intermission, the show, with many unnecessary scenes, can be a slog to sit through.

cn.t: Kirkwood's thought-provoking post-nuclear drama earns praise for its superb performances and moral complexity, though critics split on its slow pacing and creaky plotting. The stellar British cast elevates an unsettling meditation on generational responsibility.
